(AP) Jordanian prosecutors on Tuesday charged three men with terrorism-related offences over a deadly gun attack last month on a church in the kingdom's south. On October 23, gunmen killed nine people and wounded 25 others when they stormed a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Hammoud village, in Jordan's Karak governorate. Authorities said the suspected gunmen, two Jordanian brothers and their relative by marriage, fled after the attack but were arrested three days later. According to a statement from Jordan's state security prosecutor, "the public prosecution has completed all investigative procedures... related to the terrorist attack carried out at Saint George Church". The seven charges include "committing terrorist acts resulting in the death of a person, carrying out terrorist acts using weapons and ammunition, possessing weapons and ammunition for terrorist purposes, conspiring to carry out terrorist acts and promoting the ideology of a terrorist group". Under Jordan's anti-terrorism law, a conviction on the most serious charge -- carrying out terrorist acts resulting in death -- is punishable by death. Authorities have described the suspects as followers of a hardline extremist ideology. The attack shocked the kingdom, where Christians make up around three percent of Jordan's Muslim-majority population. ethiopia.title: Long After Ethiopia Completes GERD, Egypt, Sudan Invoke Nile Water Rights Under Colonial-Era Agreement
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Long After Ethiopia Completes GERD, Egypt, Sudan Invoke Nile Water Rights Under Colonial-Era Agreement - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Long After Ethiopia Completes GERD, Egypt, Sudan Invoke Nile Water Rights Under Colonial-Era Agreement 3 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Egypt and Sudan have renewed their opposition to Ethiopia's independent management of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), invoking historical Nile water-sharing agreements and demanding a binding legal framework, more than a year after Ethiopia officially inaugurated the project. The two countries reaffirmed their position in a joint statement issued on November 2 following the third round of their "2+2" consultation mechanism, bringing together foreign and irrigation ministers in Cairo, according to Egyptian local media. The statement described the two countries' water security as "indivisible" and warned that Ethiopia's operation of the dam without a binding agreement continues to threaten downstream water security. Cairo and Khartoum called on Ethiopia to abandon what they characterized as "unilateral policies" and return to negotiations based on international law, including principles of avoiding significant harm, prior notification, consultation and consensus. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The two governments also claimed that the dispute should remain confined to Egypt, Sudan and Ethiopia, rejecting attempts to involve other Nile Basin countries. The renewed position comes as Ethiopia maintains that its development of the Blue Nile is a legitimate exercise of its sovereign right to utilize natural resources for the benefit of its population, while advocating equitable and reasonable use of shared transboundary waters. The 1959 Nile Waters Agreemen t, repeatedly invoked by Egypt and Sudan , was concluded exclusively between the two countries and allocated the river's waters between them without Ethiopia's participation. Ethiopia has long rejected the agreement as a basis for restricting its rights over the Nile, arguing that arrangements reached without the participation of upstream countries cannot determine their entitlement to use shared water resources. The two countries also reaffirmed support for their Permanent Joint Technical Commission for Nile Waters and expressed conditional support for development projects in the southern Nile Basin, provided they meet technical standards and comply with notification and consultation requirements. The statement additionally addressed Sudan's political situation, expressing support for its unity and reconstruction while opposing the establishment of parallel governing entities. It also reiterated that Red Sea governance should remain the responsibility of countries bordering the sea. GERD inaugurated after 14 years of construction Ethiopia officially inaugurated the self-financed GERD in September 2025 , in Guba, Benishangul-Gumuz region, completing a project launched in 2011 and widely celebrated domestically as a landmark in national development and self-reliance. The dam, built through domestic financing, has an installed generation capacity of approximately 5,150 megawatts and a reservoir capacity of about 74 billion cubic meters, making it Africa's largest hydroelectric project. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed described the completion as a historic achievement in Ethiopia's longstanding effort to harness the Abay, or Blue Nile, for development. Ethiopia has maintained that the dam is designed primarily for electricity generation rather than water consumption, and has emphasized its potential to expand access to electricity, support regional power exports and regulate seasonal flooding downstream. Construction and filling proceeded amid years of disputes and negotiations with Egypt and Sudan, which have sought legally binding arrangements governing the dam's operation, particularly during prolonged droughts. Ethiopia, which contributes a substantial share of the Nile's flow through the Blue Nile, has consistently argued that the GERD does not deprive downstream countries of their water rights and that cooperation should be based on equitable and reasonable utilization rather than historical arrangements that excluded upstream states. Intransigence over historical agreements and equitable use Egypt and Sudan have relied on historical agreements, including the 1959 accord, to defend their "established water allocations" and press Ethiopia for a binding operational agreement. The agreement allocated 55.5 billion cubic meters annually to Egypt and 18.5 billion cubic meters to Sudan, while making no provision for Ethiopia, which was not a party to the treaty. Ethiopia has maintained that the colonial-era and bilateral arrangements are null and void and cannot override the rights of other Nile Basin countries to equitable and reasonable use of shared water resources. Negotiations over the GERD have repeatedly stalled, with Egypt insisting the involvement of the United Nations and describing Ethiopia's filling and operation of the dam as "unilateral". Ethiopia has rejected those terms and called for a cooperative approach that recognizes the development needs of all riparian states. Tensions have intensified in 2026 amid renewed Egyptian objections to Ethiopia's plans for additional Blue Nile development projects and closer diplomatic coordination between Cairo and Khartoum. ethiopia.summary: Egypt and Sudan have reiterated their opposition to Ethiopia's management of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), invoking colonial-era water-sharing agreements to assert their claims. Following a recent "2+2" consultation in Cairo, the two countries issued a joint statement emphasizing their water security as "indivisible" and warning that Ethiopia's unilateral actions threaten downstream water availability. They called for a binding legal framework and negotiations based on international law, rejecting any involvement from other Nile Basin nations. Ethiopia, which inaugurated the GERD in September 2025, argues that the dam is crucial for its development and does not infringe on the water rights of downstream countries. The historical 1959 Nile Waters Agreement, which allocated water without Ethiopia's participation, is contested by Ethiopia, which insists on equitable use of shared resources. Tensions have escalated as Egypt and Sudan seek to strengthen their diplomatic coordination against Ethiopia's development plans.

ethiopia.content: Deadly RSF drone attacks reveal deep divisions between Sudan and Ethiopia | Border Disputes News | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Middle East Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Explained Sport Opinion Video Interactives More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up Navigation menu caret-left US-Israel war on Iran Yemen conflict Middle East Africa Asia Asia Pacific Europe Latin America US & Canada caret-right News | Border Disputes Deadly RSF drone attacks reveal deep divisions between Sudan and Ethiopia Deadly drone attacks in Sudan have led to fierce diplomatic disputes with Ethiopia, exposing complex regional rivalries and fragile border security. Listen Listen (6 mins) Save Share Deadly RSF drone attacks reveal deep divisions between Sudan and Ethiopia on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Rubble left after fires at Alneam market after a drone attack in the disputed Abyei region along the border between South Sudan and Sudan, October 20, 2026 [Handout via Reuters] By Mohammad Mansour Published On 3 Nov 2026 3 Nov 2026 The Sudanese government’s allegations that Ethiopia is behind a deadly wave of unmanned aerial assaults belie a deep and longstanding rift between the two countries, which threatens to intensify internal conflicts in both. Sudan has officially lodged complaints with the United Nations Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council over allegations that the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary – which has been at war with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) since April 2023 – is using Ethiopian territory to launch attacks against civilian sites, including power stations. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 As aid situation worsens, displaced Sudanese worry about warnings of famine list 2 of 3 Sudan files complaints against Ethiopia with UN over deadly drone spree list 3 of 3 Drone attacks extend campaign targeting Sudan’s power system end of list Ethiopia’s alleged support for the RSF has triggered differences within the SAF on how to respond next, Sudanese border affairs specialist Abdul Kareem Al-Almin Ahmed told Al Jazeera. “The mutual accusations are many and almost daily, and the tension on the part of the Sudanese army has reached high levels, to the degree that made some voices inside the Sudanese army and the forces allied with it demand that Sudan declare war on Ethiopia based on these interventions,” Al-Almin told Al Jazeera. Suspected RSF drone attacks have heavily damaged civilian infrastructure in SAF-controlled areas. More than 90 percent of power stations in Sudanese cities have been rendered out of service due to drone attacks, and al-Almin said the technological capabilities of these weapons indicate significant external backing. “They are mysterious drones, drones that reach long distances, and almost all Sudanese lands are currently violated by these drones, which confirms that they are drones with a special characteristic and flight properties for a long range and have high destructive power,” Al-Almin added. A detailed report prepared by the Sudanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs alongside military intelligence claimed that 70 separate assaults involving 187 one-way attack drones were launched from Ethiopian territory between February and October. The frequency of these attacks seems to be increasing, with 28 attacks carried out by 97 drones in October. Advertisement The use of armed drones has been catastrophic for civilians in Sudan, with 13 million people already displaced and thousands at risk of famine due to the war. Between February 15 and October 27, drone attacks killed 176 Sudanese soldiers and 484 civilians, according to a report compiled by the Transitional Sovereignty Council, which is linked to the de facto Sudanese leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and the SAF. It identified Asosa Airport in western Ethiopia, the Kurmuk-Gizen border area, and the Bahir Dar airbase in Amhara as specific launch sites for drone attacks. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on Saturday he was appalled by the use of drones in the war and condemned the catastrophic toll this was having on civilians. A drone attack on displaced families in Wad el-Mahi , near the Ethiopian border on October 3, killed 26 women and four children. Another drone attack in Nyala, in Sudan’s Darfur region, on October 26 killed at least 21 people and injured at least 40. The Sudanese military has repeatedly accused the Ethiopian government of aiding the RSF. Addis Ababa denies the claims and has in turn accused the Sudanese government of backing rebels linked to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front . The tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia extend beyond these drone attacks and allegations of support for rebel groups. They also involve a confrontation over water resources and strategic regional alliances. There have been ongoing tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), built by Addis Ababa on the Nile River. Egypt and Sudan rely heavily on the Nile for water supplies and, being downstream, fear the GERD threatens their national security and claim it breaches international law. “The Sudanese-Ethiopian file is a complex file, in which many factors have intertwined: The Renaissance Dam problem first … and the rapprochement between the Sudanese army and the Egyptian government,” Al-Almin said. The Sudanese government is also angered that the RSF is allegedly receiving support from Ethiopia, he added. But Badr Hassan Al-Shafei, a professor of African studies and conflict resolution expert, said fears of an escalation that could harm Sudan and Ethiopia are preventing an all-out confrontation between the two countries. In a study published by the Al Jazeera Centre for Studies, Al-Shafei wrote that “Khartoum’s interest lies in the stability of its eastern neighbourhood to avoid security threats and waves of asylum. “Khartoum fears that providing military support to Tigray will lead to an explosion of the situation on its borders, which may increase displacement operations that the border Sudanese states cannot bear, especially in light of the continuation of the war against Hemedti,” Al-Shafei stated. Advertisement A direct military confrontation with Addis Ababa would severely strain an already exhausted Sudanese military apparatus, which is still involved in intense battles with the RSF in the southeast of the country. Ultimately, leaders of both countries recognise the catastrophic potential of expanding the battlefield beyond each other’s borders. “If the Sudanese army opens a war front with Ethiopia, this is not in its favour and confuses the region,” Al-Amin wrote. “[Sudan could find itself] fighting on two fronts: Fighting the Rapid Support Forces that occupy part of Sudan, and fighting the Ethiopian army that possesses its capabilities and the border extension capable of reaching through it.” aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement About About Show more About Us Code of Ethics Terms and Conditions EU/EEA Regulatory Notice Privacy Policy Cookie Policy Cookie Preferences Accessibility Statement Sitemap Work for us Connect Connect Show more Contact Us User Accounts Help Advertise with us Stay Connected Newsletters Channel Finder TV Schedule Podcasts Submit a Tip Paid Partner Content Our Channels Our Channels Show more Al Jazeera Arabic Al Jazeera English Al Jazeera Investigative Unit Al Jazeera Mubasher Al Jazeera Documentary Al Jazeera Balkans AJ+ Our Network Our Network Show more Al Jazeera Centre for Studies Al Jazeera Media Institute Learn Arabic Al Jazeera Centre for Public Liberties & Human Rights Al Jazeera Forum Al Jazeera Hotel Partners Follow Al Jazeera English: facebook twitter youtube instagram-colored-outline rss bluesky tiktok-colored-outline © 2026 Al Jazeera Media Network
ethiopia.summary: Recent drone attacks attributed to Sudan's Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have heightened tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia, revealing deep-rooted divisions and escalating regional conflicts. Sudanese officials have accused Ethiopia of facilitating these attacks, which have targeted civilian infrastructure, including power stations, leading to significant damage and casualties. The Sudanese government has lodged complaints with the UN Security Council and the African Union, claiming that over 70 drone assaults were launched from Ethiopian territory between February and October 2026. The situation has prompted calls within Sudan's military for a potential declaration of war against Ethiopia. Despite the rising hostilities, experts suggest that both nations are wary of a full-scale confrontation due to the potential for further destabilization. The ongoing conflict is compounded by disputes over water resources related to the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, which has strained relations between Sudan, Ethiopia, and Egypt. The humanitarian impact is severe, with millions displaced and thousands facing famine.

Ambassador Awes Hagi Yusuf Ahmed, Somalia’s National Security Advisor, said the personnel currently redeploying to Uganda are primarily bilateral forces operating under separate arrangements between the governments of Somalia and Uganda. He emphasised that the Ugandan contingent serving under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) remains in the country and continues to carry out its mandate alongside other contributing partner forces and the Somali National Army (SNA). “The redeployment of bilateral forces should not be misconstrued as a complete withdrawal of Ugandan military personnel from Somalia,” Ahmed said. The clarification follows an announcement by the Uganda People’s Defence Forces (UPDF) that it had commenced the withdrawal of troops deployed under bilateral arrangements, with the first cohort already returning to Uganda. In a statement issued on November 2, the UPDF said the bilateral withdrawal would be completed within days, while all Ugandan forces, including those serving under AUSSOM, are expected to leave Somalia by the close of 2027. Ahmed made the remarks after chairing a tripartite meeting involving the Federal Government of Somalia (FGS), AUSSOM and the United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS). During the meeting, the parties reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening the tripartite coordination mechanism to enhance cooperation, strategic planning and logistical support for AUSSOM and the Somali National Army. They also underscored the importance of sustained, predictable and adequate international support in advancing Somalia’s security transition, consolidating gains from ongoing offensive operations and strengthening the operational capacity of Somali security forces. Ahmed said continued cooperation among Somalia, its international partners and security institutions remained essential to achieving sustainable security, lasting peace and long-term stability. Uganda has maintained a military presence in Somalia for two decades, supporting peace and stabilisation efforts. The ongoing redeployment of bilateral forces is part of a broader transition towards Somali security forces assuming greater responsibility for the country’s security. somalia.summary: Somalia has clarified that the ongoing withdrawal of Ugandan troops does not mean a complete exit of all Ugandan military personnel from the country. Ambassador Awes Hagi Yusuf Ahmed, Somalia’s National Security Advisor, stated that the troops currently redeploying to Uganda are part of bilateral forces operating under separate agreements between Somalia and Uganda. He emphasized that the Ugandan contingent serving under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) remains active and continues its mission alongside the Somali National Army (SNA). This clarification follows the Uganda People’s Defence Forces (UPDF) announcement of troop withdrawals, which are expected to be completed soon, with all Ugandan forces, including those under AUSSOM, set to leave by the end of 2027. Ahmed highlighted the importance of continued cooperation among Somalia, its international partners, and security institutions to ensure sustainable security and stability in the region. Uganda has been involved in peacekeeping efforts in Somalia for two decades. (158 words)

The agreement was signed on Monday in Djibouti City by the Speaker of Somalia’s House of the People and the Speaker of Djibouti’s National Assembly, Dileita Mohamed Dileita. Under the agreement, the two parliaments will cooperate on improving legislative procedures, training parliamentary staff, conducting legal research and modernizing their institutional operations. The memorandum also provides for closer cooperation between parliamentary standing committees, the use of modern technology, improved data security and the establishment of parliamentary friendship groups between the two countries. Both sides also agreed to coordinate their positions on issues discussed at regional and international parliamentary forums. Following the signing ceremony, Dileita welcomed the outcome of discussions with the Somali delegation, saying the exchange of views had produced positive results for both countries. The Somali parliamentary speaker said Mogadishu was committed to strengthening ties with Djibouti through knowledge-sharing and institutional cooperation. The agreement is part of broader efforts by the two neighboring countries to expand bilateral relations and strengthen cooperation between their government institutions. Privacy Policy Terms of Service Search Somalia Rejects Israel’s Accreditation of Ambassador in Hargeisa November 3, 2026 2 min read By - Editor-in-Chief Asha Elmi MOGADISHU, 3 November 2026 – Somalia has condemned Israel’s accreditation of an ambassador in Hargeisa and the laying of a cornerstone for an embassy in Somaliland, calling the moves a violation of its sovereignty. Somalia’s statement, issued on Tuesday, followed a ceremony at the presidential palace in Hargeisa where Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi Irro, received the credentials of Israel’s ambassador to Somaliland, Michael Lotem. The Somaliland presidency announced the ceremony. Somalia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the actions were taken without the federal government’s consent and amounted to “a flagrant violation of Somalia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and unity.” “Somalia rejects them as null and void and without legal effect,” the ministry said. The statement said that Hargeisa and the Somaliland region remain part of Somalia. It added that under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, opening diplomatic relations and permanent missions requires the consent of the sovereign state. Somalia’s foreign ministry said the latest steps compound Israel’s recognition of Somaliland in December 2025. The African Union, the regional bloc IGAD, the Arab League and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation have all rejected that recognition. The ministry warned that, with insecurity rising in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, actions that encourage fragmentation and disregard internationally recognised borders risk deepening tensions across the region. Somalia demanded that Israel immediately reverse the measures. It called on other states and international organisations to reject them and to avoid any engagement that would give them legitimacy. The federal government said it reserves the right to take diplomatic, political and legal measures under international law. somalia.title: African Union Somalia Bases Plan Follows Uganda Exit - kulu-media.com
somalia.content: African Union Somalia Bases Plan Follows Uganda Exit | Kulu Media Home Latest News Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea Sudan Africa World Politics Economy Finance Business Education More Analysis Entertainment Tech Health Sports English English ትግርኛ አማርኛ Connect with us Search Kulu Media African Union Plans to Secure Four Somalia Bases as Ugandan Troops Withdraw Home Latest News Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea Sudan Africa World Politics Economy Finance Business Education More Analysis Entertainment Tech Health Sports English English ትግርኛ አማርኛ Home » News » Africa » Horn of Africa » African Union Plans to Secure Four Somalia Bases as Ugandan Troops Withdraw Horn of Africa African Union Plans to Secure Four Somalia Bases as Ugandan Troops Withdraw African Union peacekeepers prepare to secure four bases near Mogadishu. Published 52 seconds ago on November 3, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk Ugandan troops serving under the African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) stand in formation as the mission's force commander inspects a guard of honour during a medal ceremony. File photo. Credit: AMISOM Public Information / Wikimedia Commons The African Union mission in Somalia plans to take control of four strategic military positions near Mogadishu as Ugandan troops withdraw from the country, according to newly reported details of an official mission letter. The move is intended to prevent Al-Shabaab militants from exploiting security gaps in southern Somalia. The African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) will redeploy peacekeepers to Sabiid-Anole, Bariire, Awdheegle and Bulonagad in the Lower Shabelle region during troop rotations scheduled for November 2026. According to an Associated Press report published on November 3, the plan was outlined in an October 31 letter from AUSSOM to the United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS). The letter identifies the four positions as strategically important to Mogadishu’s security and proposes transferring African Union personnel from the coastal town of Barawe to reinforce them. The new arrangements follow Uganda’s decision to begin withdrawing troops deployed under a bilateral security agreement with Somalia, raising concerns about the ability of Somali and African Union forces to maintain control of areas previously secured by Ugandan units. As previously reported by Kulu Media , the African Union had warned that Uganda’s departure could leave parts of southern Somalia vulnerable to Al-Shabaab attacks. Four Strategic Positions Near Mogadishu The four positions identified for African Union control are located in Lower Shabelle, a region that has experienced repeated fighting between Somali government forces and Al-Shabaab militants. The October 31 letter describes the locations as critical to protecting Mogadishu and preventing militants from exploiting gaps created by the withdrawal of Uganda’s bilateral troops. AUSSOM intends to reposition personnel currently serving in the Barawe sub-sector, approximately 220 kilometers southwest of Mogadishu, to the four locations. A detailed account published by The Somali Digest on November 3 identifies the letter as reference AUSSOM/HOM/22/044.26. According to that account, AUSSOM asked UNSOS to recognize Sabiid-Anole, Bariire, Awdheegle and Bulonagad as new mission locations and continue providing logistical assistance to the redeployed peacekeepers. The request also calls for the Barawe sub-sector to be reclassified as locations outside the African Union mission’s operational structure. However, the letter does not specify which forces will assume responsibility for all the positions being vacated in Barawe. That uncertainty raises questions about whether the redeployment will strengthen defenses closer to Mogadishu while creating additional security responsibilities farther south. Uganda Begins Withdrawal Under Two Separate Arrangements Uganda announced on November 2 that it had begun withdrawing military personnel from Somalia, ending the first phase of a deployment that has supported counterinsurgency operations for nearly two decades. Ugandan military spokesperson Colonel Chris Magezi confirmed that the first group of troops had returned home and that personnel serving under the bilateral agreement were expected to complete their withdrawal within days. Uganda also contributes thousands of soldiers to AUSSOM, but those personnel are operating under a separate African Union mandate. The broader withdrawal of Ugandan forces, including its African Union peacekeeping contingent, is planned to proceed gradually through the end of 2027. A Reuters report confirmed that Uganda had begun its phased departure after almost 20 years of military involvement in Somalia. The October 31 AUSSOM letter explains that Uganda deployed additional bilateral troops following an April 2025 summit in Entebbe, where African leaders discussed strengthening security around Mogadishu. Those forces subsequently participated in operations to recover and hold territory previously controlled or contested by Al-Shabaab. The decision to withdraw the bilateral contingent has therefore required the African Union mission to reconsider how it distributes its remaining forces. Questions Remain Over Security in Barawe The proposed redeployment could create a difficult security transition in Barawe, a strategically important coastal town that Somali and African Union forces recovered from Al-Shabaab in 2014. The town is also the official capital of Somalia’s South West State. According to the Associated Press, Somali army commander Major General Ibrahim Mohamed Mohamud visited military personnel in Barawe on November 2 and instructed them to remain vigilant and intensify operations against Al-Shabaab. However, the army’s statement did not clarify whether Somali national forces would assume responsibility for all the African Union positions being vacated. The Somali Digest separately reported claims from local security sources that Ugandan troops had handed positions in Barawe and Shalanbood to Somali forces. Those reported handovers had not been officially confirmed by AUSSOM or Somalia’s federal government at the time of reporting. The distinction is important because the African Union’s plan to take over four positions near Mogadishu does not automatically establish that the security arrangements for Barawe and surrounding areas have been completed. Funding Shortages Complicate Security Transition The redeployment is taking place amid continuing financial and logistical challenges facing the African Union mission. Farhan Isak Yusuf, deputy executive director of the Mogadishu-based research organization Somali Public Agenda, told the Associated Press that funding shortages had contributed to the pressure surrounding Uganda’s withdrawal. He also warned that Somali national forces face resource limitations while confronting an insurgency that continues to threaten government-controlled territory. AUSSOM relies heavily on international assistance for transportation, fuel, medical evacuation, communications and other essential operational requirements. The October 31 letter specifically requests continued UNSOS logistical support for the four positions that the African Union intends to occupy. The mission’s financial difficulties have raised concerns about its ability to maintain existing deployments while supporting Somalia’s transition toward greater national responsibility for security. The issue also affects other countries contributing personnel to the African Union mission, including Ethiopia, whose military presence in Somalia remains important to regional counterinsurgency cooperation. Somalia has sought to maintain its neutral position amid growing tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Uganda’s decision is a separate development and should not be interpreted as confirmation that other troop-contributing countries have adopted similar withdrawal plans. Al-Shabaab Threat Remains a Central Concern Al-Shabaab, an Al-Qaeda-linked militant organization, continues to carry out attacks against Somali government forces, African Union troops and civilian targets. Lower Shabelle remains particularly important because of its proximity to Mogadishu and its network of roads connecting the capital to southern Somalia. The group’s ability to conduct attacks in contested areas has made the security transition especially sensitive. The African Union’s decision to reinforce four positions reflects concern that withdrawing experienced troops without suitable replacements could create opportunities for militants to regain influence. However, there has been no independently verified evidence that Al-Shabaab has captured the four positions as a direct result of Uganda’s latest withdrawal. Somalia is also dealing with political disagreements between federal authorities and regional administrations, adding pressure to the government’s efforts to coordinate security operations. The challenge is not limited to replacing departing troops. It also involves ensuring that Somali forces have sufficient personnel, equipment, logistical support and political coordination to maintain security over time. African Union Faces Difficult Decisions Over Remaining Forces The planned transfer of peacekeepers to Sabiid-Anole, Bariire, Awdheegle and Bulonagad represents an immediate operational response to Uganda’s withdrawal. It also illustrates the difficult choices facing AUSSOM as the mission attempts to protect strategic areas while preparing for a gradual reduction in foreign military involvement. The four positions are expected to receive African Union personnel during November’s troop rotations, but questions remain about the timing of the handovers, the future of the Barawe bases and the availability of continued international support. For Somalia, the outcome will depend on whether the redeployment successfully prevents security gaps without weakening other areas where Al-Shabaab remains active. The African Union’s latest plan offers a proposed solution for four strategically important positions, but it does not yet resolve the broader challenges surrounding Uganda’s military departure and Somalia’s long-term security transition. (AP Photo/Farah Abdi Warsameh, File) The African Union’s security mission in Somalia has warned that Uganda’s troop withdrawal could leave parts of southern Somalia vulnerable to attacks by Al-Shabaab, raising concerns about the future of counterinsurgency operations as Kampala begins ending nearly two decades of military involvement in the country. The warning was contained in an October 31 letter from the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) to the United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS), according to a Reuters report published on November 2, 2026. Two diplomatic sources verified the letter, which identified potential security gaps in the Lower Shabelle region, where Ugandan troops have supported Somali forces in operations against the Al-Qaeda-linked militant group. The warning comes as Uganda confirms that its military has begun a phased withdrawal from Somalia, starting with troops deployed under a separate bilateral security agreement with the Somali government. Uganda People’s Defence Forces (UPDF) spokesperson Chris Magezi said the first contingent of soldiers had already returned home. The military confirmed that the withdrawal would eventually include Ugandan personnel serving under AUSSOM, with the entire process expected to be completed by the end of 2027. Uganda currently has approximately 4,500 troops deployed under the African Union mission, although the number of additional soldiers serving under bilateral arrangements has not been publicly established. African Union Raises Concerns Over Security Gaps The African Union mission’s warning highlights the risk that areas previously secured by Ugandan and Somali troops could become vulnerable if international forces leave before Somali security institutions are prepared to assume full responsibility. Lower Shabelle has been a major focus of military operations against Al-Shabaab, with Ugandan forces supporting efforts to recover strategic towns and disrupt militant positions. The region includes important routes connecting Mogadishu with other parts of southern Somalia, making its security particularly significant for the federal government’s counterinsurgency campaign. Ugandan forces have participated in operations around towns including Sabiid-Anole, Bariire and Awdhegle, where Somali authorities have sought to consolidate control following military offensives. However, maintaining security in recovered areas remains a challenge because Al-Shabaab continues to conduct attacks against government forces, African Union personnel and civilian targets. The AUSSOM letter identifies potential vulnerabilities resulting from the withdrawal. It does not establish that Al-Shabaab has launched a new offensive or captured additional territory following Uganda’s announcement. Uganda Confirms Phased Withdrawal After Nearly 20 Years Uganda first deployed troops to Somalia in 2007 as part of the African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM), becoming one of the earliest and most significant contributors to international security operations in the country. Its forces helped push Al-Shabaab militants out of major urban areas, including parts of Mogadishu, and subsequently supported operations across southern Somalia. The mission evolved from AMISOM into the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (ATMIS) before AUSSOM began operations in January 2025. According to the Associated Press , Uganda’s military confirmed on November 2 that the first group of soldiers had returned home under the phased withdrawal arrangement. Thousands of Ugandan troops remain deployed, and their departure is expected to take place gradually rather than through an immediate removal of all personnel. The distinction between Uganda’s bilateral deployment and its African Union mission forces is important. The initial withdrawal affects troops deployed through the bilateral arrangement, while the broader plan also envisages the eventual departure of Uganda’s AUSSOM contingent. Somali State Minister for Foreign Affairs Ali Omar acknowledged the potential consequences of an abrupt withdrawal. Speaking to Reuters, Omar said the current situation was not critical but warned that a sudden departure of Ugandan troops could create security problems. His comments indicate concern about the timing and coordination of the transition rather than confirmation of an immediate collapse in security. Somalia Faces Growing Pressure to Assume Security Responsibilities Uganda’s withdrawal comes at a sensitive moment for Somalia, where the federal government is seeking to strengthen national security institutions while continuing its campaign against Al-Shabaab. The militant organization remains capable of carrying out bombings, ambushes and attacks on military and civilian targets despite years of operations by Somali forces and their international partners. The departure of experienced Ugandan units could increase pressure on Somali security forces to hold territory, protect major transport routes and prevent militants from exploiting security gaps. The transition is also taking place amid financial uncertainty surrounding international support for the African Union mission. In September, the United States agreed to provide additional time for the United Nations to wind down logistical assistance to AUSSOM, as previously reported by Kulu Media . That arrangement provides temporary relief but does not resolve the mission’s longer-term funding and logistical challenges. UNSOS supplies essential services, including transportation, fuel, medical assistance, communications and other operational support to African Union personnel and Somali security forces. Any reduction in troop numbers or logistical assistance could complicate security operations unless alternative arrangements are established. Political Divisions Complicate Somalia’s Security Transition The withdrawal also coincides with political disagreements between Somalia’s federal government and opposition groups over constitutional reforms, elections and the distribution of political authority. The closure of the United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia on October 31 has added to concerns about the country’s political transition. Although the political mission has ended, UN humanitarian agencies and separate logistical support arrangements remain active. Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has repeatedly emphasized the need for stronger national institutions and continued international cooperation against Al-Shabaab. In a recent interview with Sky News, covered by Kulu Media, Mohamud defended his government’s security strategy and discussed Somalia’s relationships with neighboring countries. He also reaffirmed that Somalia would remain outside any potential confrontation between Ethiopia and Eritrea, as detailed in Kulu Media’s report . The president has presented Somalia’s long-term security strategy as one combining military operations, efforts to counter extremist ideology and measures to disrupt militant financing. However, political divisions between federal and regional authorities could complicate the coordination required to maintain security as international forces gradually withdraw. Withdrawal Raises Questions About Future Operations Against Al-Shabaab Uganda’s planned departure represents a significant transition for Somalia’s security architecture after almost two decades of military cooperation. The African Union’s warning underscores concerns that a poorly coordinated withdrawal could weaken security in areas where Al-Shabaab remains active. For Somalia, the central challenge will be ensuring that national forces can assume responsibility for areas currently protected by international troops without creating opportunities for militant groups to regain influence. The timetable extends through the end of 2027, giving Somali authorities, Uganda and the African Union time to coordinate the transition. However, the effectiveness of that process will depend on the readiness of Somali security forces, continued logistical support and political cooperation between the country’s institutions. No new Al-Shabaab territorial gains directly resulting from Uganda’s withdrawal had been independently confirmed at the time of reporting. somalia.summary: The African Union (AU) plans to secure four military bases in Somalia as Ugandan troops begin their withdrawal, which raises concerns about potential security gaps that could be exploited by Al-Shabaab militants. The bases, located near Mogadishu in the Lower Shabelle region, are critical for maintaining security in the area. The African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) intends to redeploy peacekeepers to Sabiid-Anole, Bariire, Awdheegle, and Bulonagad during troop rotations scheduled for November 2026. Uganda's withdrawal, which has been ongoing since November 2, marks the end of nearly two decades of military involvement in Somalia. The AU has warned that this departure could leave southern Somalia vulnerable to attacks. The transition is complicated by financial and logistical challenges faced by AUSSOM, raising questions about the ability of Somali forces to maintain security in the absence of Ugandan troops. The situation underscores the ongoing threat posed by Al-Shabaab and the need for effective coordination among Somali and AU forces.

somalia.content: Somalia Produces Just 5% of Estimated Annual Fishery Capacity - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia Produces Just 5% of Estimated Annual Fishery Capacity Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday November 3, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somalia produces about 30,000 tonnes of fish annually, just 5% of its estimated marine fishery production capacity of 600,000 tonnes, according to a report by The EastAfrican, as the country seeks to attract investment into its underdeveloped fishing industry. Abdi Dirshe, director general of Somalia's Ministry of Fisheries and Blue Economy, said the gap between current output and estimated capacity stands at nearly 570,000 tonnes a year. Dirshe estimated that the sector could generate between $1.8 billion and $3 billion in annual revenue and create more than 210,000 jobs if its resources were properly developed. The figures represent potential economic returns rather than existing industry revenue or employment. Somalia has approximately 3,333 kilometres of coastline, but inadequate fishing equipment, limited processing and storage facilities, and security concerns have restricted the industry's development. Investment and fisheries policy Expanding production would require investment in fishing vessels, equipment, landing sites, cold storage, processing plants and export infrastructure. Abdullahi Adan, coordinator of Somalia's Sustainable Fisheries Development Project, known as Badmaal, said the government's National Transformation Plan 2025–2029 prioritises private investment, market development and public-private partnerships in the sector. Somalia has introduced legal and regulatory measures intended to encourage investment, including an Investment Law, a public-private partnership policy, a Fisheries Law and food safety regulations. Local companies have also begun investing in fish processing and boatbuilding, with projects aimed at creating jobs and developing technical skills among young Somalis. Export markets and security challenges Engineer Ali Ibrahim Siyad, chairman of the Somali Fish Exporters Association, said quality assurance and seafood certification are essential for gaining access to international markets. He identified the United States, China, the Middle East and East African countries as potential destinations for Somali fish exports. However, exporters face difficulties meeting the requirements of international markets, while the industry continues to operate with limited infrastructure and equipment. Fisheries expert Omar Abdulle Hayle said security remains the primary consideration for investors seeking to protect their personnel and assets. The report also identified limited capacity to protect marine resources as an obstacle to developing the industry. Fisheries experts called for transparent management and stronger marine environmental protection alongside efforts to increase production. somalia.title: U.S. bombs Iranian island; Israel blocks aid through Rafah; Turkey strikes Al-Shabaab in Somalia - Drop Site News
somalia.content: U.S. bombs Iranian island; Israel blocks aid through Rafah; Turkey strikes Al-Shabaab in Somalia Subscribe Sign in Drop Site Daily U.S. bombs Iranian island; Israel blocks aid through Rafah; Turkey strikes Al-Shabaab in Somalia Drop Site Daily: November 3, 2026 Drop Site News Nov 03, 2026 305 6 61 Share A limited number of trucks carrying humanitarian aid cross from Egypt toward the Gaza Strip on February 8, 2026. Photo by Ahmed Sayed/Anadolu via Getty Images. Tuesday, November 3, 2026 – Iran: U.S. strikes Iran’s Qeshm Island. U.S. and Iran far from peace deal; Qatar intensifies mediation ahead of midterms. IRGC claims capture of two U.S. spy drones over Qeshm Island. Three oil tankers hit mines in Strait of Hormuz; Indian sailor killed in separate ship attack. Talks with Saudi Arabia continue, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says, calling for regional security without foreign forces. Palestine: Four Palestinians killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza. Israel orders complete closure of Gaza crossing with Egypt, blocking aid and commercial goods. In Gaza, 42% of essential medicines, 50% of medical supplies depleted. Israel orders seizure of 11 acres of Palestinian land in occupied West Bank. Israeli forces demolish shops as settlers torch property across West Bank. Yemen: Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted drone over Mecca; Ansarallah denies launching attack. Saudi strikes kill 17 civilians; Ansarallah strike kills five civilians at health center. Saudi Aramco expands repeatedly attacked oil pipeline. Lebanon: Israel again violates ceasefire in southern Lebanon. France investigating Israeli attack on Beirut apartment building as possible war crime. U.S.: Midterm elections nationwide. The Guardian: ICE re-arrests immigrants who won release from detention. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani demands ICE stop using city property to stage operations. Supreme Court rejects Trump administration attempt to force California to set aside 20,000 mail-in ballots. Judge dismisses DOJ’s case against Harvard. President Donald Trump says he would consider preemptive pardons for Elon Musk, other allies. New York Times: Trump administration preparing to scale back pregnancy-related workplace protections. FEMA directs disaster aid to Republican districts in California and Minnesota ahead of midterms. U.S. to remove South Africa, Rwanda from African trade program. New York child is first to die of measles in the state in 30 years. International: Al-Shabaab attack in Somalia kills four civilians. Turkish airstrikes against Al-Shabaab in Somalia kill two civilians. Russia attacks aid site, killing 31, and hospital, injuring 73. UK increases wait time for most foreign workers seeking permanent residency to 10 years. Ebola death toll in central and eastern Africa tops 5,300; most cases in the Congo. Attackers ambush police convoy in Nigeria, killing 8 personnel. Northern Ethiopia conflict pushing health system toward collapse, WHO says. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio talks reforms with Venezuelan officials. This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday Subscribe Iran U.S. strikes Iran’s Qeshm Island: The U.S. carried out strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island on Monday as part of a series of unannounced attacks conducted in recent weeks, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing U.S. officials. The officials described the operations as defensive, claiming that Iranian forces had fired a surface-to-air missile at a U.S. fighter jet and launched another missile toward commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Washington has deliberately kept quiet about the strikes to avoid signaling a return to major combat operations, one official said. The revelations contradict President Donald Trump’s public portrayal of the conflict as largely dormant. “We haven’t been doing any fighting for months,” he told reporters on Monday. He also denied plans to attack Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections. Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said on Tuesday that Tehran retains the right to self-defense until U.S. military attacks end “completely and permanently.” The Israeli military denied involvement in the reported strikes. U.S. and Iran far from peace deal; Qatar intensifies mediation ahead of midterms: Iran and the United States remain far apart on an agreement to end their war, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Tuesday, as Qatar intensified mediation efforts to prevent renewed escalation after the U.S. midterm elections. Qatari mediators traveled to Tehran on Monday night to discuss a revised proposal, with both sides expected to respond within 36 hours. Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari said that both countries were reviewing the proposal. “If there were no glimmer of hope, there would be no negotiations,” he said, adding that “as a mediator, we cannot lose hope.” Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said that Tehran had delivered a “strong, rational response” to Washington. “The ball is now in Washington’s court,” he said. Meanwhile, Trump claimed that Iran wanted a settlement “as soon as possible,” and suggested a deal “could happen,” even as he threatened to strike Iran’s suspected nuclear facility at Pickaxe Mountain “in one hour.” Vice President JD Vance said that U.S. negotiators engaged Iran in “a number of good conversations,” adding that he felt “pretty good about the prospects” of reaching a negotiated settlement. IRGC claims capture of two U.S. spy drones over Qeshm Island: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Tuesday that its Aerospace Force brought down two U.S. MQM-170 reconnaissance drones over the southern island of Qeshm Island. To date, the IRGC claims to have captured four U.S. drones of this type. Three oil tankers hit mines in Strait of Hormuz; Indian sailor killed in separate ship attack: Three oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire while traveling through unauthorized routes in the Strait of Hormuz, the IRGC said on Tuesday. The IRGC claimed that the vessels had switched off their identification systems before entering “restricted” waters, triggering explosions that left them burning along the strait’s southern shores. Separately, on Monday, an Indian sailor was killed when the Indian-flagged cargo vessel MSV Al Jusufi came under attack near Limah, off Oman’s coast. India’s Shipping Minister said that the remaining 13 crew members were rescued by the Omani Coast Guard. No actor has claimed responsibility for the attack. Talks with Saudi Arabia continue, Iran’s Araghchi says, calling for regional security without foreign forces: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Tuesday that Tehran harbors no hostility toward Gulf Cooperation Council countries, and that it seeks new regional security arrangements led by countries in the region, without foreign military involvement. In a post on X referencing his interview with Al Jazeera, Araghchi praised the “positive role” played by Qatar and Oman, and said that Iran continues its dialogue with Saudi Arabia. “Our goal is to reach new regional security arrangements established by the countries of the region themselves, away from any foreign military presence,” he wrote. Palestine Four Palestinians killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza: An Israeli drone strike on a police post near the College of Applied Sciences, west of Khan Younis in southern Gaza, killed three Palestinians and wounded several others on Tuesday, WAFA reported. One police officer was among those killed in the attack, according to the Interior Ministry in Gaza. The ministry condemned the strike, saying that it was part of ongoing Israeli attacks on police and security forces in Gaza. Separately, a man died of wounds sustained in an earlier strike northwest of Khan Younis. Over the past 24 hours, Israeli attacks killed six Palestinians—five due to new attacks, and one due to wounds sustained in an earlier attack—and injured 27 others across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health. The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023, has risen to 74,615 killed and 175,899 injured. Since October 11, 2025, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,599 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 5,774, while 847 bodies have been recovered. Exclusive: Israel orders complete closure of Gaza crossing with Egypt, blocking aid and commercial goods: Israel informed the UN and Egyptian committee on Monday evening that it is imposing a “complete and comprehensive closure” of the Rafah crossing, blocking humanitarian aid, commercial shipments, food, fuel, and cooking gas entering Gaza through the Egyptian route, a senior Palestinian source involved in negotiations told Drop Site News. Israel claimed that alleged smuggling and “interference by government bodies in the Gaza Strip” were the reasons for the closure, the source said. The Egyptian route handles approximately 50 to 60 trucks daily, the source said, adding that “fuel and gas come entirely through this route.” Under the October 2025 ceasefire agreement, 600 aid trucks are supposed to enter Gaza daily, but Israel has severely restricted deliveries, allowing an average of only around 200 trucks per day. The closure comes as Palestinians across Gaza face the onset of winter in makeshift tents and heavily damaged homes, with worsening food insecurity compounded by cuts to UN food assistance and rising prices. Read Abdel Qader Sabbah’s report on the dire conditions in Gaza for Drop Site here . In Gaza, 42% of essential medicines, 50% of medical supplies depleted: Forty-two percent of essential medicines and 50% of medical supplies are completely out of stock, Gaza’s Health Ministry said on Tuesday, bringing critical healthcare services closer to total collapse. The depletion of chemotherapy drugs, hormonal treatments, immunosuppressants, and clotting factors disrupted 55% of treatment protocols for thousands of patients, the ministry said, exposing them to life-threatening complications as Israeli restrictions obstruct treatment outside Gaza. Israel orders seizure of 11 acres of Palestinian land in occupied West Bank: Israeli authorities issued military orders to seize approximately 45 dunams (11 acres) of Palestinian land across the occupied West Bank. In the northern Jordan Valley, Israeli forces ordered the seizure of seven dunams in Khirbet Al-Hadidiya to construct a military road, following earlier land seizures and the establishment of a settlement outpost in the area. In Jenin, two orders dated October 28 target 11.2 dunams in Deir Abu Daif and Qabatiya to construct roads and buffer zones around the Ganim and Kadim settlements, which Israel reestablished this year after evacuating them in 2005. Near Ramallah, another order targets 26.5 dunams in Deir Nizam, Umm Safa, and Atara for a road linking settlements. The orders, which remain in effect until the end of 2028, would expand Israeli military control, restrict Palestinian access to agricultural land, and strengthen infrastructure connecting Israeli settlements, the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said. Israeli forces demolish shops as settlers torch property across West Bank: Hebron: Israeli forces demolished five shops belonging to a Palestinian resident, northwest of Hebron, on Tuesday, WAFA reported. Forces also detained the Al Jazeera correspondent Muntaser Nassar and more than 20 Palestinians during raids in Dura, reportedly binding and mistreating them before releasing them. In Yatta, south of Hebron, Israeli settlers set fire to two vehicles, an agricultural storage room, and a house under construction, and spray-painted racist slogans. Bethlehem: Israeli forces assaulted Palestinians harvesting olives in Khalayel Al-Louz, southeast of Bethlehem, and prevented them from continuing their harvest. Nablus: Israeli settlers severely beat a 60-year-old Palestinian man in Burqa, northwest of Nablus, leaving him hospitalized. In Majdal Bani Fadel, south of Nablus, settlers set fire to two vehicles parked outside Palestinian homes. Ramallah and Al-Bireh: Israeli forces arrested Luay Nawaf, head of the Ein Yabrud village council, after raiding his home east of Ramallah. Yemen Saudi coalition says it intercepted drone over Mecca; Ansarallah denies launching attack: The Saudi-led coalition claimed on Tuesday that it intercepted a drone over the Mecca region. Ansarallah military spokesperson Yahya Saree denied that Yemeni forces had carried out any operations targeting Saudi territory that day, accusing Riyadh of fabricating the incident. Saree called the allegation that the Ansarallah had targeted the Islamic holy city of Mecca “an old lie revived,” claiming Saudi Arabia was attempting to distract from battlefield defeats. Saudi strikes kill 17 civilians; Ansarallah strike kills five civilians at health center: Saudi airstrikes killed 17 civilians over two days, most of them children, Sana’a Health Ministry said on Tuesday, accusing Saudi forces of targeting homes, residential neighborhoods, and markets. Separately, an Ansarallah ballistic missile struck Al-Saqiyah Health Center in Lahj province on Monday, killing five people, including three medical workers, and wounding 15 others, according to Yemen’s Saudi-backed government. Saudi Aramco expands repeatedly attacked oil pipeline: Saudi Arabia oil giant Aramco began expanding its East-West crude pipeline and developing additional export routes to bypass the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, CEO Amin Nasser said on Tuesday. Saudi Arabia aims to increase pipeline export capacity to as much as 10 million barrels per day, up from the East-West pipeline’s current capacity of 7 million. The key pipeline has been attacked several times since September, with Saudi Arabia blaming an Iraqi armed group for a strike and Ansarallah claiming responsibility for others. Lebanon Israel again violates ceasefire in southern Lebanon: Israeli forces launched multiple attacks across southern Lebanon on Tuesday, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency. Bint Jbeil: Israeli forces shelled the outskirts of Bra’shit. Nabatieh: Israeli forces set fire to homes in Zawtar Al-Sharqiya, and carried out an airstrike on the outskirts of Kfartabnit. Marjeyoun: Israeli forces carried out an explosion in the town of Qantara, accompanied by machine-gun fire. France investigating Israeli attack on Beirut apartment building as possible war crime: Two judges in the crimes against humanity unit of the Paris Judicial Court were appointed to investigate an Israeli airstrike on a 12-story residential building in central Beirut on November 26, 2024, that killed seven civilians, including the parents of French-Lebanese artist Ali Cherri, AFP reported. Cherri, whose parents were 87 and 77, filed a complaint this year with the International Federation for Human Rights. His lawyer described the judicial investigation as a first involving alleged Israeli war crimes in Lebanon. “What happened to my parents is not an isolated case,” Cherri told AFP. “I hope this investigation will help break the impunity enjoyed by Israeli officials responsible for attacks against civilians in Lebanon and Palestine.” U.S. News Midterm elections nationwide: U.S. voters will head to the polls on Tuesday with control of both houses of Congress on the line and with several key Senate races – in Michigan, Texas, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa, Maine and Alaska — garnering particular attention. Recent polling indicates that Democrats are likely to take over the House and are leading in most (if not all) contested Senate races. Drop Site will be hosting a joint livestream with Breaking Points, available on both YouTube feeds; coverage begins at 6 p.m. here . The Guardian: ICE re-arrests immigrants who won release from detention: The Guardian found at least 20 cases of immigrants who won their release from detention and were later detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Immigrants have filed more than 91,000 habeas petitions since January 2025, per ProPublica , more than during the past three administrations combined. Attorneys link many re-detentions to the Trump administration’s push for third-country deportations, with more than 25,000 people already sent to third countries. Mamdani demands ICE stop using city property to stage operations: New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani demanded that ICE stop using city-owned lots during its enforcement actions. On Monday, the mayor’s office sent a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin , acting ICE Director David Venturella , and New York ICE field office head Kenneth Genalo , saying “ICE has no right to use our property as a base for tearing families apart.” The letter added, “if they keep coming back, we will see them in court.” Mamdani’s demand comes after ICE shot a man while he was in his car with his five-year-old son on October 8 in upper Manhattan. Supreme Court rejects Trump administration attempt to force California to set aside 20,000 mail-in ballots: On Monday, the Supreme Court denied the Trump administration’s emergency application to set aside 20,000 mail-in ballots in California. The ruling was swift, coming hours after the administration filed an emergency request. The case follows the Justice Department’s declaration in October that it had compiled a list of more than 20,000 likely noncitizen voters in California. That list appeared to be riddled with errors, according to California officials, with only 7,035 names carrying Los Angeles County addresses and others confirmed as U.S.-born citizens. Judge dismisses DOJ’s case against Harvard: Massachusetts U.S. District Judge Myong Joun granted Harvard University’s motion to dismiss the Justice Department’s case against it. The DOJ had accused the university of withholding admissions data from investigators seeking to determine if it was in compliance with the Supreme Court’s 2023 ban on affirmative action in admissions. The government failed to prove that it had tried to resolve the dispute with the school before suing it, the court found. Joun did not rule on the merits of the case, meaning that the government can reopen its complaint once it addresses procedural deficiencies. Trump says he would consider preemptive pardons for Elon Musk, other allies: In a New York Post interview released Monday, President Trump called supposed Democratic threats against Elon Musk , including arrest and nationalizing SpaceX, just “talk,” but said “we just have to protect those people.” Asked by columnist Miranda Devine about preemptive pardons for Musk and others, he said “I would if I needed to, sure,” adding “I’d do it. I did it for J6,” referring to clemency for more than 1,500 Capitol riot defendants. Democratic leaders have discussed investigating Musk’s business practices, but have not called for his arrest. Musk, whose net worth hovers around $1 trillion, has spent nearly half a billion dollars on Republican candidates and groups during the 2026 midterms. NYT: Trump administration preparing to scale back pregnancy-related workplace protections: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, under chair Andrea Lucas , plans to narrow work accommodations for pregnant workers, the New York Times reported. As early as this month, the EEOC could release a proposal that scants the implementation of the 2022 Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, which covers such worker protections as bathroom and water breaks, reprieve from heavy lifting, and time off for prenatal care. The law includes accommodations for “related medical conditions,” such as abortions, fertility treatments, and care for endometriosis and menstruation. FEMA directs disaster aid to Republican districts in California and Minnesota ahead of midterms : On October 30, the Federal Emergency Management Agency directed tens of millions of dollars to several Los Angeles, Calif., churches and to projects in or near vulnerable
somalia.summary: On November 3, 2026, the U.S. conducted airstrikes on Iran's Qeshm Island, claiming defensive measures against Iranian missile threats. This escalation occurs amid stalled peace negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, with Qatar mediating to prevent further conflict. Concurrently, Israel has intensified its military actions in Gaza, resulting in the deaths of four Palestinians from recent airstrikes, while also imposing a complete closure of the Rafah crossing, halting humanitarian aid and essential supplies. The situation in Gaza is dire, with significant shortages of medical supplies reported. In the West Bank, Israel has ordered the seizure of Palestinian land for military purposes, further exacerbating tensions. Meanwhile, Turkey has targeted Al-Shabaab in Somalia, resulting in civilian casualties. The ongoing violence and humanitarian crises highlight the complex geopolitical landscape in the region, with various nations involved in military actions and negotiations.

football.summary: يستعد الهلال السوداني لمواجهة رايون سبورت الرواندي غداً الأربعاء، في الجولة الثامنة من الدوري الرواندي الممتاز. يسعى الفريق لتعزيز موقعه في جدول الترتيب بعد سلسلة من الانتصارات. المدير الفني جوزيف زينباور، الذي أنهى عقوبة إيقافه، يخطط للاعتماد على تشكيلته الأساسية، رافضاً تكرار تجربة الدفع بالبدلاء التي أدت إلى خسارة ثقيلة أمام مارين. من المتوقع أن يشارك اللاعبون الأساسيون مثل مصطفى كرشوم وياسر عوض وأرنست لوزولو، مع التركيز على الانضباط التكتيكي والتنظيم الدفاعي. تعتبر هذه المباراة اختباراً مهماً للهلال قبل انطلاق دور المجموعات في دوري أبطال أفريقيا، حيث سيواجه حوريا كوناكري الغيني في 28 نوفمبر. تُقام المباراة على ملعب كيغالي بيليه في الساعة السادسة والنصف مساءً، وقد استأنف الهلال تدريباته في كيغالي وسط أجواء من الحماس والتركيز.

football.summary: مباراة الهلال السوداني ضد هورويا في دوري أبطال أفريقيا، التي أقيمت في 27 نوفمبر 2026، انتهت بالتعادل السلبي 0-0. هذه المباراة كانت جزءًا من مرحلة المجموعات للموسم 2026/2027، حيث يتنافس الفريقان ضمن المجموعة A. لم يتمكن أي من الفريقين من تسجيل الأهداف، مما أثر على رصيد النقاط لكليهما في البطولة. في سياق آخر، يواجه الهلال السوداني تحديات في تحضيراته للمجموعات، حيث أثرت بعض الأحداث على استعداداته. كما أن هناك تقارير تشير إلى أن نجم الهلال يقترب من تحقيق إنجاز خاص، مما يضيف المزيد من التوتر والإثارة حول أداء الفريق في المباريات القادمة. يتطلع الهلال السوداني إلى تحسين أدائه في المباريات المقبلة لتعزيز فرصه في التأهل إلى الأدوار المتقدمة.

football.summary: تواجه الهلال السوداني فريق بيراميدز في مباراة ضمن دوري أبطال إفريقيا، حيث انتهت المباراة بالتعادل السلبي 0-0. أقيمت المباراة في 8 يناير 2027، وهي جزء من مرحلة المجموعات للموسم 2026/2027. يتواجد الهلال السوداني في المجموعة A، التي تضم أيضًا الترجي الرياضي التونسي وبيترو أتلتيكو ونواذيبو. على الرغم من عدم تسجيل أي أهداف، إلا أن المباراة كانت مثيرة، حيث حاول كلا الفريقين السيطرة على مجريات اللعب. الهلال السوداني يسعى لاستعادة توازنه بعد سلسلة من النتائج المتباينة في الدوري الرواندي، بينما بيراميدز يأمل في تحسين أدائه في البطولة. تتواصل المنافسات في دوري أبطال إفريقيا، حيث يتطلع كل فريق لتحقيق نتائج إيجابية في المباريات القادمة لتعزيز فرصه في التأهل إلى الأدوار المتقدمة.

السوداني الممتاز كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' أشعلت جماهير الهلال السوداني منافسة خاصة بين نجوم الفريق، مصطفى كرشوم وأرنست لوزولو وياسر عوض، للفوز بجائزة "أفضل لاعب في شهر أكتوبر" التي خصصتها إدارة النادي لتحفيز اللاعبين ورفع مستوى أدائهم. ويعد المدافع مصطفى كرشوم المرشح الأبرز لنيل الجائزة بفضل مستواه المتميز الذي قدمه خلال الشهر الماضي، لا سيما في مباراتي سيداما بونا الإثيوبي بالدور التمهيدي الثاني لمسابقة دوري أبطال أفريقيا، مما جعله يحظى باهتمام واسع من الجماهير، وتقدم اللاعب بوضوح مكتسحًا زميليه مقتربًا من تحقيق مكسب مهم قبل صدامات قارية مرتقبة. في المقابل، يواصل ياسر عوض حضوره القوي في المنافسة للشهر الثاني على التوالي، بعد أن كان مرشحًا بارزًا في شهر سبتمبر/ أيلول الماضي. ونجح اللاعب المحلي في قلب الطاولة على المحترف الكونغولي ستيفن إيبويلا وأزاحه عن مركز الظهير الأيمن، ليستأثر بفرصة المشاركة بصفة أساسية بعد أن كسب ثقة المدرب جوزيف زينباور. اقرأ أيضًا بعد رسائل الحزم.. مدرب الهلال يتلقى دعما قبل مواعيد حاسمة الهلال السوداني يستعيد توازنه بفوز ثمين في الدوري الرواندي بدوره، فرض أرنست لوزولو نفسه ضمن قائمة المرشحين بعد أن نجح في تسجيل هدف رائع في شباك سيداما بونا الإثيوبي، مقدمًا مستويات باهرة، ومسهمًا في تحقيق فريقه لانتصارات محلية وقارية. كرشوم يواصل تألقه مع الهلال السوداني من جانبه، يمثل مدافع الهلال السوداني مصطفى كرشوم ظاهرة نادرة في الملاعب السودانية، لاستمرار تألقه ومحافظته على مستواه مع المنتخب وفريقه، مما جعله ضمن قائمة أفضل اللاعبين في البلاد خلال السنوات الأخيرة. ورغم بلوغه سن الـ35، يتطلع اللاعب لظهورٍ لافت في الموسم الحالي، خاصة مع اقتراب دخوله الفترة الحرة، طامحًا في الحصول على تقييم يتناسب مع موهبته وخبراته، واغتنام فرصة التجديد الأخيرة قبل اعتزاله. من المتوقع أن تعلن إدارة النادي عن الفائز بالجائزة في حفلٍ مصغر دأبت على إقامته دوريًا. مع العلم أنّ المحترف الموريتاني في صفوف الفريق، أحمد سالم مبارك، كان قد توج بالجائزة عن شهر سبتمبر/ أيول الماضي وسط حفاوة كبيرة من زملائه، فيما يعد مصطفى كرشوم المرشح الأوفر حظا لنيل الجائزة عن شهر أكتوبر. النشرة البريدية اشترك معنا بالنشرة البريدية لتصلك آخر أخبار الرياضة الأول مع الفريق عقب انضمامه إليه مؤخراً. وتألق في اللقاء صانع الألعاب عبد الرؤوف يعقوب، الذي توج بجائزة "رجل المباراة" بفضل مستواه المتميز وإسهاماته الفاعلة في تحقيق الفوز. اقرأ أيضًا.. الهلال السوداني يستحضر ذكرى لا تنسى في الدوري الرواندي زينباور يتحرك وقرارات حاسمة تهز الهلال السوداني من جهة أخرى، يستعد رفاق القائد محمد عبد الرحمن لخوض سلسلة من التحديات الصعبة في الفترة المقبلة؛ حيث football.summary: استعاد الهلال السوداني توازنه بفوز ثمين على غاسوجي الرواندي بنتيجة 2-0 في الجولة السابعة من الدوري الرواندي، الذي يشارك فيه الهلال إلى جانب المريخ. جاء هذا الفوز بعد خسارة مفاجئة في الجولة السابقة، حيث أظهر الفريق أداءً قوياً. سجل المدافع بابي ديارا أول أهدافه الرسمية مع الفريق، بينما أضاف القائد محمد عبد الرحمن هدفاً آخر، مستمراً في تألقه بعد تسجيله ثنائية في دوري أبطال أفريقيا. شهدت المباراة أيضاً عودة الجناح أداما كوليبالي بعد إصابة طويلة، وظهور المهاجم إيفان نانا لأول مرة. تألق صانع الألعاب عبد الرؤوف يعقوب، الذي حصل على جائزة "رجل المباراة". يستعد الهلال لمواجهة تحديات صعبة في الفترة المقبلة، بما في ذلك مباراة ضد رايون سبورت الرواندي، قبل بدء دور المجموعات في دوري أبطال أفريقيا.

football.content: بعد رسائل الحزم.. مدرب الهلال يتلقى دعما قبل مواعيد حاسمة بعد رسائل الحزم.. مدرب الهلال يتلقى دعما قبل مواعيد حاسمة مباريات اليوم رياضات كرة القدم الأخبار فيديو البطولات البرامج دول بعد رسائل الحزم.. مدرب الهلال يتلقى دعما قبل مواعيد حاسمة من مباراة الهلال ضد غاسوجي (facebook/alhilalsc.official) 1 نوفمبر 2026 بعد رسائل الحزم.. مدرب الهلال يتلقى دعما قبل مواعيد حاسمة الهلال السوداني دوري أبطال أفريقيا محمد عبد الرحمن الغربال عبد الرؤوف يعقوب كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' تنفس مدرب الهلال السوداني جوزيف زينباور الصعداء، بعدما استعاد فريقه توازنه سريعا وحقق الفوز على منافسه "غاسوجي" الرواندي، عقب الخسارة الثقيلة التي تعرض لها في الجولة الماضية. وحققت إدارة النادي مكاسب مهمة قبل الاستحقاقات الحاسمة، بفضل خطط مدروسة شملت مواصلة تدعيم صفوف الفريق بمحترفين أجانب، والاستعداد لتلبية مطالب المدرب بشأن إحداث تغييرات جذرية في التشكيلة. وأسهمت هذه الخطوات في إشعال المنافسة بين اللاعبين، ما انعكس إيجابا على مستويات عدد من النجوم الذين استعادوا بريقهم وتألقهم. رسائل واضحة تعيد التألق إلى كبار نجوم الهلال أسهم منح إدارة النادي الضوء الأخضر للمدرب زينباور لإجراء تغييرات متواصلة على قائمة الفريق واستبعاد بعض العناصر، في توجيه رسائل واضحة إلى النجوم بضرورة تطوير مستوياتهم وتقديم الأفضل لضمان مكانهم في التشكيلة. وظهرت نتائج هذه السياسة سريعا، بعدما توج صانع الألعاب عبد الرؤوف يعقوب بجائزة أفضل لاعب في المباراة الأخيرة. من جانبه، استعاد القائد محمد عبد الرحمن حسه التهديفي، بعدما سجل 3 أهداف في آخر 3 مباريات، وقدم مستويات مميزة استثمر خلالها الفرص التي منحها له المدرب، ليؤكد جاهزيته ويصبح خيارا مثاليا قبل انطلاق مرحلة المجموعات من دوري أبطال أفريقيا . كما استعاد المهاجم أداما كوليبالي مكانه في صفوف الفريق بتوقيت مثالي، قبل خوض المنافسات الأفريقية، ليمنح زينباور إضافة نوعية، باعتباره أحد الركائز الأساسية التي أسهمت في الطفرة التي حققها الهلال خلال السنوات الأخيرة. اقرأ أيضًا الهلال السوداني يستعيد توازنه بفوز ثمين في الدوري الرواندي زينباور يتحرك بعد السقوط المدوي.. قرارات حاسمة تهز الهلال وسارع زينباور إلى منح لاعبه المالي مزيدا من الفرص، تمهيدا لعودته إلى الظهور القاري هذا الموسم بعد غياب طويل بسبب الإصابة، ليكون أحد أبرز الخيارات المطروحة لإحداث تغيير في تشكيلة الفريق خلال مواجهة الافتتاح أمام حوريا كوناكري الغيني. ويعلق جمهور الهلال آمالا كبيرة على مواصلة التألق في البطولة الأفريقية، وتجاوز عقبة الدور ربع النهائي التي توقفت عندها مسيرة الفريق في النسختين الأخيرتين، أملا في الذهاب بعيدا في المنافسة هذه المرة. وينتظر الفريق تحد شاق أمام حوريا كوناكري يوم 28 نوفمبر/تشرين الثاني الجاري، ضمن الجولة الأولى من منافسات المجموعة الرابعة، قبل أن يحل ضيفا على المغرب الفاسي بين 4 و6 ديسمبر/كانون الأول، ثم يستضيف بيراميدز المصري في قمة الجولة الثالثة بين 18 و20 من الشهر نفسه. النشرة البريدية اشترك معنا بالنشرة البريدية لتصلك آخر أخبار الرياضة اشترك معنا دول كرة القدم الأخبار الدوريات الفرق رياضات التنس كرة السلة رياضات ميكانيكية
